questions.stimulus:
ENL teacher's intake notes on four grade 8 ELLs who enrolled in the district this month
Student | Background | Home-language literacy and math
Student 1 | Age 13, from Ukraine; continuous schooling; Entering on the NYSITELL | Reads Ukrainian at grade level; math at grade level
Student 2 | Age 13, transferred from a NYC school she has attended since kindergarten | Reads Spanish about two years below grade level
Student 3 | Age 14, from Guatemala; first time in U.S. schools; his rural school had no math teacher for his last three years there | Reads Spanish at about grade level; math about three years below grade level
Student 4 | Age 14, from China; first time in U.S. schools; continuous schooling | Reads Mandarin at grade level; math about one year below grade level
questions.stem: Based on the NYS definition, which student should be identified as a Student with Inconsistent/Interrupted Formal Education (SIFE)?
options: Student 1
Student 2
Student 3
Student 4
questions.why: NYS defines SIFE as ELLs who have attended U.S. schools for less than 12 months and who, on initial enrollment, are two or more years below grade level in home-language literacy and/or math because of interrupted or inadequate schooling. Student 3 qualifies: he is new to U.S. schools, and three years without math instruction left him about three years below grade level in math. Because the definition says 'and/or,' a math gap alone is enough even though his Spanish reading is on grade level. Limited English alone never makes a student SIFE.

traps.note: Student 1 is a newcomer at the Entering level, but her schooling was continuous and her home-language literacy and math are on grade level. Limited English alone does not make a student SIFE.

She is two years below grade level in Spanish reading, but she has attended U.S. schools for years. SIFE applies only to ELLs with under 12 months in U.S. schools whose gaps come from interrupted or inadequate schooling.
Math one year below grade level does not meet the 'two or more years below' threshold, and his home-language literacy is on grade level, so he does not meet the NYS criteria.

questions.key: SIFE: under 12 months in U.S. schools and 2+ years below grade level in home-language literacy or math (either is enough) due to interrupted schooling.

questions.stem: A district enrolls a 15-year-old whose family reports that she has had several years of interrupted schooling. A counselor asks how NYS sequences her identification. Which statement is accurate?
options: She first goes through ELL identification (HLQ, interview, and NYSITELL); SIFE screening follows, since only ELLs can be SIFE
SIFE screening replaces the NYSITELL for students with interrupted schooling, since an English test can't show what she knows
SIFE status is decided through a re-identification review, which teachers may request after observing her classwork for 45 school days
SIFE status is assigned at enrollment based on the family's report, since interrupted schooling is the defining feature of SIFE
questions.why: Being an ELL is part of the SIFE definition, so NYS requires the usual Part 154 identification first: the HLQ, the interview in English and the home language, and the NYSITELL, within 10 school days. Only then does the school determine SIFE status, within 30 school days of initial enrollment, using the oral interview questionnaire and, for certain languages, the Multilingual Literacy SIFE Screener (MLS). A family's report starts the inquiry, but SIFE status requires evidence of a gap of two or more years in home-language literacy and/or math.

traps.note: SIFE screening doesn't replace ELL identification. She still goes through the HLQ, interview, and NYSITELL; the SIFE determination comes after she is identified as an ELL.

Re-identification (within 45 school days) lets a parent, a teacher (with parent consent), or a student 18 or older question ELL status itself. SIFE status is a separate determination made within 30 school days.

A family's report of interrupted schooling starts the inquiry but doesn't establish status. SIFE requires ELL status plus evidence (the oral interview questionnaire and, where available, the MLS) of a gap of two or more years.

questions.key: Only ELLs can be SIFE: complete ELL identification (HLQ, interview, NYSITELL) first, then determine SIFE status within 30 school days of enrollment.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old SIFE from rural Honduras attended school for about two years and is beginning to read in Spanish and English. Her grade 9 ENL teacher is choosing reading materials for her. Which choice best meets her needs?
options: Kindergarten picture books with simple patterned text, since they match her current decoding level in English
Short, high-interest nonfiction on age-appropriate topics with controlled language, plus explicit foundational skills work
The grade 9 class novel with an audio recording, so that she reads the same text as her peers without separate materials
Phonics worksheets and decodable word lists until she decodes fluently, followed by a gradual move to connected text
questions.why: Adolescent SIFE need foundational literacy taught explicitly, but through materials that respect their age and build background knowledge: high-interest, age-appropriate texts with controlled language (often called hi-lo texts). Pairing skill instruction with meaningful content lets literacy and content knowledge grow together and keeps an older student engaged.

traps.note: The text level may fit, but the content is meant for five-year-olds. Adolescent SIFE need materials that respect their age and build the background knowledge high school requires.
Giving her the same novel as everyone else ignores her profile. With about two years of schooling, a dense grade 9 novel is far beyond what she can access, even with audio.
Foundational skills matter, but drilling them apart from meaningful text delays comprehension and content learning and tends to disengage older students.

questions.key: Adolescent SIFE: teach foundational literacy explicitly through age-appropriate, high-interest texts with controlled language, never baby books.

questions.stimulus: Observation notes, grade 8 ENL class: Several SIFE students participate eagerly when the class plans a school garden together, talking through which plants to grow and how to care for them. During individual worksheets that ask them to sort unfamiliar vocabulary words into abstract categories, the same students stop working or copy from one another.
questions.stem: Which next step best reflects the Mutually Adaptive Learning Paradigm (MALP) developed for SIFE?
options: Replace the written worksheets with group discussions, since SIFE learn best through oral, collaborative tasks
Keep assigning the individual worksheets daily, so the students adjust to the independent work U.S. schools expect
Practice classifying abstract shapes and nonsense words first, so that the thinking skill is learned apart from content
Have the group sort the plants they chose into categories, then have each student complete and explain a chart
questions.why: MALP (DeCapua & Marshall) asks teachers to meet SIFE partway: accept students' conditions for learning (immediate relevance, interconnectedness); combine their processes with school processes (shared responsibility with individual accountability, oral transmission with the written word); and introduce new academic tasks, such as classification, through familiar language and content. Sorting the plants the group chose and then completing an individual chart does all three.

traps.note: MALP combines oral transmission with the written word; it does not drop writing. Removing written tasks lowers expectations and withholds the literacy practice SIFE need.
This expects only the students to adapt. MALP is mutually adaptive: the teacher bridges students' familiar ways of learning to school tasks instead of treating them as a problem.
MALP introduces new academic tasks through familiar content and language. Practicing classification with meaningless material strips away the relevance that makes the task learnable.

questions.key: MALP: teach new academic tasks through familiar content, and combine group work with individual accountability and oral work with written work.

questions.stimulus: Teacher note, grade 6: Moussa, age 11, speaks Wolof and arrived from Senegal in September after about one year of formal schooling. He arrives late to class after lunch, does not open his binder or copy the homework from the board, and stands up to leave whenever a bell rings, even in the middle of an activity.
questions.stem: Which response by the ENL teacher is most appropriate?
options: Explicitly teach and model school routines, such as reading a visual schedule, using a binder, and responding to bells
Apply the school's tardiness and preparedness consequences consistently, so he learns expectations the way classmates do
Refer him to the pre-referral team, since trouble following multistep routines can be a sign of an executive-function disorder
Excuse him from homework and binder expectations until he reaches the Transitioning level on the NYSESLAT
questions.why: Many SIFE have had little chance to learn the 'hidden curriculum' of school: schedules, bells, binders, copying assignments, and homework routines. These are learnable skills, so the best response teaches them explicitly with visuals, modeling, practice, and peer support. Punishing, pathologizing, or excusing the student would all leave the skills untaught.

traps.note: His classmates have had years to learn these routines; Moussa has had about one. Consequences for skills no one has taught him punish his background instead of addressing it.
His behavior is fully explained by limited prior schooling. Not yet knowing routines he has never been taught is not evidence of a disability.
School routines can be learned now with support. Excusing him delays skills he needs and signals low expectations.

questions.key: SIFE may not know school routines yet; teach the 'hidden curriculum' explicitly instead of punishing, excusing, or referring.

questions.stem: A district with a grade 7 Spanish Transitional Bilingual Education (TBE) program enrolls a 12-year-old SIFE from El Salvador who has had about three years of schooling and is beginning to read in Spanish. At the parent orientation, her mother asks whether her daughter would learn English faster in ENL alone. Which response best reflects research on literacy development?
options: Under NYS rules a SIFE must be placed in TBE until she reaches grade-level literacy in Spanish, and then she may move to ENL
ENL alone is the better choice for SIFE, since instruction in Spanish would divide her limited learning time between two languages
Literacy and content learned in Spanish transfer to English, so TBE can support her progress, though the choice is the family's
She should build spoken English first, since learning to read Spanish before speaking English would cause interference between them
questions.why: Cummins' Common Underlying Proficiency and Developmental Interdependence hypotheses hold that literacy and concepts learned in the home language transfer to English. For a SIFE who is just beginning to read, building literacy in a language she already speaks is an efficient route to academic English, which is why bilingual programs often benefit SIFE. Under Part 154, though, parents choose the program after orientation; no rule forces a SIFE into TBE.

traps.note: No NYS rule forces SIFE into TBE. Under Part 154, parents choose among the program options after the orientation.
This is the 'time on task' myth. Research shows that home-language literacy supports English literacy rather than competing with it, especially for students still learning to read.

This misreads transfer. Reading skills learned in Spanish, such as decoding, comprehension strategies, and concepts of print, transfer positively to English; they don't need to wait for spoken English.

questions.key: Home-language literacy transfers to English (Cummins' CUP), so bilingual programs can help SIFE, but parents still choose the program.

questions.stimulus: Teacher note, grade 8 math: Mateo, age 13, speaks Mixteco and some Spanish and attended school in Oaxaca for about three years. During a classroom store simulation, he calculated totals and change in his head faster than any classmate, explaining his steps in Spanish. He left a page of written multi-digit subtraction problems blank.
questions.stem: Which instructional step best builds on this evidence?
options: Start him on grade 2 math worksheets to fill the gaps in written computation before he rejoins grade-level work
Have him explain his mental strategies, then link each step to written notation using money and manipulatives
Assign daily timed drills on multi-digit subtraction until his written accuracy matches his speed in mental calculation
Reassess his skills with an English word-problem test to determine his true grade-level placement in mathematics
questions.why: Mateo's quick mental math is a fund of knowledge (Moll): real number sense developed outside school. His gap is written notation and school algorithms, not mathematical reasoning. Having him verbalize his strategies and then map them onto written symbols in concrete, familiar contexts bridges what he knows to what school expects, while keeping grade-level reasoning in play.

traps.note: He has strong number sense; his gap is notation. Grade 2 worksheets ignore his reasoning, remove him from grade-level math, and are age-inappropriate.
Timed drills practice the written algorithm apart from meaning and add pressure, while skipping the bridge between what he already knows and the written form.
An English word-problem test would measure his English reading, not his math. It would hide the very strength the store simulation revealed.

questions.key: Build SIFE math on real-life number sense: have students explain mental strategies, then connect them to written notation in concrete contexts.

questions.stem: A grade 6 newcomer from Uzbekistan who speaks Uzbek and some Russian joins an ENL class in October at the Entering level. Which plan for his first weeks is most appropriate?
options: Ask him to introduce himself to the class in English on his first day, so that he starts producing English right away
Seat him at a separate table with an English vocabulary workbook until he is able to follow whole-class instruction
Correct his pronunciation each time he speaks English, so that his early errors do not turn into fossilized habits
Pair him with a peer buddy, give him a visual schedule, and accept gestures and home-language responses at first
questions.why: Newcomers at the Entering level, many in a silent period, need a welcoming, low-anxiety start (Krashen's affective filter): predictable routines, visuals, a peer buddy (ideally one who shares a language), and ways to take part before they can speak English. Home-language use is an asset, and comprehensible input in meaningful classroom activity builds survival and classroom English quickly.

traps.note: A public English speech on day one ignores the silent period typical of Entering students and raises the affective filter.
Isolating him with a workbook cuts him off from interaction and comprehensible input, the very things that build English fastest.
Constantly correcting a beginner's pronunciation raises anxiety and discourages him from speaking; meaning comes before form at this stage.

questions.key: Newcomers: a welcoming, low-anxiety start (buddy, visuals, routines) that accepts nonverbal and home-language participation during the silent period.

questions.stem: A Karen-speaking refugee family that a resettlement agency recently placed in Utica enrolls three children. The ENL teacher wants to learn about the children's prior schooling and the family's needs. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Ask the oldest child, who speaks the most English, to interpret at the intake meeting so that the family feels at ease
Work with the family's resettlement caseworker and a trained Karen interpreter, asking about schooling, strengths, and goals
Ask the parents for proof of each child's immigration status before enrollment, so that the district can confirm eligibility
Send the enrollment information home in English, since refugee parents usually prefer to leave school matters to teachers
questions.why: Resettlement caseworkers, community liaisons, and trained interpreters are key partners for refugee families. They help the school learn about prior schooling (often in camp schools), health needs, and family priorities while honoring the family's right to communicate in its own language. A strengths-focused intake builds trust; children should never interpret, and enrollment never depends on immigration status.

traps.note: Children should never interpret school matters; it shifts adult responsibilities onto them and risks inaccurate or filtered information. The family is entitled to a qualified interpreter.
Under Plyler v. Doe, schools may not deny or condition K–12 enrollment on immigration status, so demanding proof of status is inappropriate.
This assumes refugee parents don't want to be involved and ignores their right to information in a language they understand. Deferring to teachers is not disinterest.

questions.key: With refugee families, partner with resettlement agencies and trained interpreters, ask about strengths and schooling, and never use children to interpret.

questions.stimulus:
Teacher log, grade 5 Integrated ENL: Farid, age 10, arrived from Afghanistan four months ago and speaks Pashto.
Week 1: Covered his ears and crawled under his desk during a fire drill.
Week 2: Put his head down and stopped responding when the room got loud during group work.
Week 3: Shoved a classmate who came up behind him in line; afterward he was calm and apologetic.
Ongoing: Smiles, engages, and reads eagerly during one-on-one sessions with the classroom aide.
questions.stem: Which interpretation and response are best supported by the log?
options: The behaviors suggest an attention or behavior disorder, so the teacher should request a special education evaluation
The behaviors show culture shock, which usually fades with time, so the teacher should wait for the adjustment stage
The behaviors may be stress responses, so the teacher should build predictability, preview drills, and consult the counselor
The shoving incident calls for the standard disciplinary consequence, so that Farid learns the same rules as all his peers
questions.why: Startling at alarms, shutting down in noise, and reacting to someone approaching from behind are common fight-flight-freeze responses after adversity, and his engagement one-on-one shows he learns well when he feels safe. A trauma-informed response adds safety and predictability (previewing drills, consistent routines, a calm-down space) and brings in school mental-health staff, rather than punishing, pathologizing, or simply waiting.

traps.note: Four months after arrival, these behaviors have a likely explanation in his recent experiences, and he engages well one-on-one. Jumping to a disability evaluation mislabels a probable stress response.

Culture shock involves frustration and homesickness during adjustment. Startling at alarms and reacting to someone behind him look more like stress responses, and simply waiting leaves him unsupported.
A standard consequence ignores the likely cause (a startle response) and can heighten his sense of threat. Expectations stay, but the response should build safety and teach regulation.

questions.key: Read newcomer behaviors through a trauma-informed lens: build safety and predictability and involve mental-health staff before punishing or referring.

questions.stem: A grade 9 ENL teacher whose class includes several refugee and asylum-seeking students plans a personal narrative unit around the prompt 'Write about your journey to the United States.' Which revision best reflects trauma-informed practice while keeping the unit rigorous?
options: Offer a choice of narrative topics, such as a meaningful person, place, or tradition, so each student decides what to share
Keep the prompt as written, since writing about hard journeys helps students process trauma and builds empathy in the class
Replace the narrative with a fill-in-the-blank paragraph about favorite foods, so that no emotional topics come up at all
Give the journey prompt only to students who came as immigrants, and assign the refugee students a separate grammar exercise
questions.why: Trauma-informed practice gives students voice and choice and never requires them to disclose painful experiences. A menu of narrative topics keeps the genre, the standards, and the writing demands intact while letting each student control how much personal history to share. A student who wants to write about the journey still can.

traps.note: Drawing on students' lives is asset-based, but requiring a trauma narrative can retraumatize students. Processing trauma is clinical work, not a writing assignment.
Dropping the genre to avoid the prompt lowers expectations. Students can write a full narrative without being required to disclose painful experiences.
This singles out refugee students, assumes all of them are traumatized, and removes them from grade-level narrative writing.

questions.key: Trauma-informed writing: offer topic choice so students control what they disclose, and keep the genre and the rigor.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes trauma-informed practice with newcomer ELLs, including refugees?
options: Teachers assume that all refugee students have experienced trauma and adjust their academic expectations downward
Teachers screen students for post-traumatic stress disorder and provide therapy as a regular part of ENL instruction
Teachers postpone academic content for students affected by trauma until counselors report a full recovery
Teachers ask 'What happened to you?' rather than 'What is wrong with you?' and build safety, predictability, and trust
questions.why: Trauma-informed practice shifts the question from 'What's wrong with you?' to 'What happened to you?' Teachers create safety, predictability, choice, and strong relationships while keeping expectations high. They don't diagnose or treat trauma (that is the role of counselors and clinicians), and they don't assume every refugee is traumatized.

traps.note: Refugee experiences vary widely, and many students are highly resilient. Assuming trauma and lowering expectations overgeneralizes about a group.
Trauma-informed teachers create supportive conditions and refer students to counselors; diagnosing and treating trauma is the work of mental-health professionals.
Withholding academic content until a 'full recovery' denies grade-level learning. Engaging, predictable learning is itself supportive.

questions.key: Trauma-informed means 'What happened to you?': safety, predictability, choice, relationships, and high expectations; teachers support and refer, not diagnose.

questions.stimulus:
Dialogue journal entry, grade 7 ELL from Ukraine (Transitioning level):
'Ms. R, in the night I have bad dreams about the sirens. I sleep maybe 3 hours. My father is still in Kharkiv and every day I check my phone for him. Please don't tell my mother I am sad, she is very worry already.'
questions.stem: Which response by the teacher is most appropriate?
options: Write back promising to keep the entry private, since protecting the student's trust in the journal comes first
Ask follow-up questions in the journal about the sirens and her father, so that she can work through the experience in writing
Reply with empathy, explain honestly that the school counselor will also see the entry in order to help, and follow school protocol
Refer her to the Committee on Special Education, since her sleep and mood problems may signal an emotional disability
questions.why: Nightmares, severe sleep loss, and constant worry are signs that the student needs support beyond the classroom. The teacher's role is to respond with empathy, avoid probing, and connect her to school mental-health staff (a counselor or social worker) through the school's protocol, telling her honestly who will see the entry and why. Teachers shouldn't promise secrecy when a student's well-being is at stake, and a stress reaction to war is not, by itself, grounds for a special education referral.

traps.note: Trust matters, but promising secrecy when a student shows signs of significant distress keeps her from support the school is responsible for providing.
Dialogue journals build language and relationships; they are not a therapy tool. Probing for details can deepen distress, and the teacher is not trained to treat it.
A stress reaction to war and fear for her father calls for counseling support, not a special education evaluation.

questions.key: When a student discloses distress, respond with empathy, don't probe or promise secrecy, and connect her to school mental-health staff.

questions.stimulus:
Grade 10 Stand-alone ENL, both students at the Entering level
Olena (Ukrainian): continuous schooling; completed algebra and chemistry in Ukraine; reads Ukrainian and Russian at grade level.
Hamid (Dari): about three years of schooling in Afghanistan; reads Dari at about a grade 3 level; a strong oral storyteller.
Plan: During independent work, both students will use the same English picture dictionary and the same beginner phonics packet.
questions.stem: Which revision to the plan best reflects the two students' profiles?
options: Keep the shared materials but assign Olena more pages each day, since both students are at the same English proficiency level
Give Olena content materials with bilingual glossaries, and give Hamid foundational literacy through age-appropriate content
Move Olena into general education classes without ENL, since her strong prior schooling will let her pick up English on her own
Focus both students on spoken English for now, and postpone reading and writing until each one reaches the Transitioning level
questions.why: Newcomers at the same English level can have very different schooling. A student with strong prior education (Olena) can transfer her literacy and content knowledge to English, so she needs English for content she already knows, with home-language supports. A SIFE (Hamid) needs explicit foundational literacy and background knowledge, taught through age-appropriate content and built on his oral strengths. Planning by proficiency level alone ignores prior schooling, a key learner variable.

traps.note: Planning by English level alone ignores prior schooling. More phonics pages don't use Olena's literacy and content knowledge, and they don't give Hamid explicit, supported literacy instruction.
An Entering student is entitled to the full ENL units of study under Part 154. Strong prior schooling speeds her progress, but it doesn't replace ENL.
Delaying literacy wastes Olena's transferable reading skills and Hamid's time; both can build English reading and writing alongside speaking from the start.

questions.key: Same English level, different schooling: use well-schooled newcomers' transferable knowledge; build SIFE foundations through age-appropriate content.

questions.stimulus: Grade 2 teacher's notes, October: Valentina arrived from Colombia in August after completing first grade in Bogotá, where she learned to read in Spanish. Her ENL teacher reports that she reads grade-level Spanish text fluently and retells it in detail. In English, she knows most letter names but confuses short vowels (she reads 'bit' as 'beet' and 'cup' as 'coop') and decodes slowly. NYSITELL level: Emerging.
questions.stem: The classroom teacher asks whether Valentina should be referred for a reading disability evaluation. Which response is best supported by the evidence?
options: Refer her, since slow English decoding after two months of instruction is an early sign of dyslexia that needs prompt evaluation
Do not refer; fluent Spanish reading and Spanish-based vowel errors signal a language difference that calls for explicit phonics
Postpone the question until she has had five to seven years to develop academic English, and then consider an evaluation
Do not refer, but place her in the Tier 3 intensive reading group with the students who scored lowest on the grade 2 screening
questions.why: A disability affects learning in every language, so the most important clue is how the student performs in her home language. Valentina reads grade-level Spanish fluently, and her English errors come straight from Spanish's five-vowel system, in which i sounds like the vowel in 'beet' and u like the vowel in 'coop.' That is a language difference, not a disability. She needs explicit English phonics, especially vowel contrasts, that builds on the reading skills that transfer from Spanish, with her progress monitored.

traps.note: Dyslexia would also affect her Spanish reading, which is strong. Two months of English instruction is far too little to judge, and her errors match the Spanish vowel system.

Cummins' CALP timeline describes typical academic-language growth; it is not a waiting period before evaluation. Here the evidence already points to a language difference, so the issue is instruction, not timing.

Grouping her with the lowest scorers by score alone ignores why she scored low. She needs targeted teaching of English vowel contrasts that builds on her Spanish literacy, not the most intensive tier.

questions.key: Strong home-language reading plus L1-pattern errors in English signals a language difference: teach English phonics that builds on transfer, and don't refer.

questions.stimulus:
Pre-referral team notes, grade 4
Nusrat (Bengali) has attended U.S. schools since kindergarten. NYSESLAT: Emerging in grades 1, 2, and 3.
Mother (through a Bengali interpreter): Nusrat spoke her first words much later than her siblings and still struggles to learn the Bengali alphabet in weekend classes.
Tier 2: 14 weeks of small-group, evidence-based reading intervention with ENL support; her progress is far below that of Bengali-speaking ELLs with similar schooling who received the same intervention.
Hearing and vision screenings: passed.
questions.stem: A team member suggests waiting two more years, since academic English takes five to seven years to develop. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Agree, since Cummins' research on academic language shows that ELLs should not be evaluated before about seven years in U.S. schools
Add ENL minutes and repeat the same Tier 2 intervention for another 14 weeks, and then revisit the question of an evaluation
Refer her for a comprehensive evaluation in Bengali and English, since her difficulties span both languages despite good instruction
Refer her for a speech-language evaluation conducted only in English, since English is the language of instruction in her classes
questions.why: Several converging data points suggest a possible disability rather than typical second-language development: delays in home-language development reported by the parent, difficulty learning to read Bengali, little progress compared with true peers despite targeted intervention, and normal hearing and vision. Waiting would be a harmful delay; nothing in IDEA or Part 154 makes ELLs wait a set number of years. The evaluation must be in her home language as well as English.

traps.note: Cummins' 5–7 year estimate describes typical academic-language growth; it is not a rule about when ELLs may be evaluated. Using it this way delays help for a student whose data already point to a disability.
More support sounds reasonable, but the data already show weak response to appropriate intervention plus home-language difficulties. Repeating the cycle is a harmful delay of a warranted evaluation.
IDEA requires evaluation in the child's native language. An English-only evaluation can't separate a disability from limited English proficiency.

questions.key: Difficulties in both languages plus weak response compared with true peers despite good instruction: refer now, with evaluation in the home language.

questions.stem: A grade 3 ELL whose home language is Mandarin is struggling in reading. Which observation would most strongly suggest that his difficulties may stem from a disability rather than from second-language acquisition?
options: He mixes Mandarin and English words in the same sentence when talking with bilingual classmates
He leaves off past-tense -ed endings in English; Mandarin verbs do not change form to show tense
He said very little English during his first months in school, though he followed class routines
His parents report the same trouble learning to read Chinese when he attended school in Shanghai
questions.why: A disability affects learning in every language, so difficulties that also appeared during home-language schooling, as reported by parents or shown in home-language work, are a major warning sign. Code-switching, L1-transfer errors such as missing past-tense endings, and an early silent period are all normal features of second-language development.

traps.note: Code-switching is a normal, rule-governed bilingual skill, not a sign of confusion or disorder.
This is negative transfer from Mandarin, which signals time with time words and particles rather than verb endings. It's a predictable second-language error, not a disability marker.
A silent period while following routines is typical of beginners, who build comprehension before they speak.

questions.key: Disabilities show up across languages and settings; code-switching, transfer errors, and silent periods are normal L2 development.

questions.stimulus:
Grade 3 universal screening: English oral reading fluency (words correct per minute)
Group | Fall | Winter | Gain
Luis (Spanish; Emerging; second year in U.S. schools) | 38 | 58 | +20
Spanish-speaking ELLs at Emerging with similar schooling (average) | 40 | 61 | +21
All grade 3 students (average) | 85 | 104 | +19
Winter benchmark: 97 words correct per minute
questions.stem: Luis's classroom teacher wants to refer him for a special education evaluation because his score is far below the benchmark. Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: Luis is growing at the same rate as his true peers, so the data do not suggest a disability; he needs continued support and monitoring
Luis scores about 40 words below the grade 3 benchmark, so the size of the gap by itself shows that an evaluation is needed now
Luis's gain matches the grade 3 average, so he no longer needs any additional language or literacy support this school year
Luis should move into Tier 3 intervention, since any student this far below the benchmark needs the most intensive support available
questions.why: For ELLs, the key comparison is with true peers: students with a similar home language, English proficiency, and schooling who received similar instruction. Luis started low and remains below the benchmark, but he is growing at the same rate as his true peers (and the grade), which is the expected pattern for an Emerging ELL. A gap in level without a gap in growth does not suggest a disability.

traps.note: A gap in level is expected for an Emerging ELL. Without a gap in growth compared with true peers, low scores alone do not suggest a disability.
His growth is healthy, but he still reads far below the benchmark. He needs continued language and literacy support to close the gap.
This applies one cut score to everyone and ignores his profile. His growth matches his true peers', so the priority is strong core instruction with ENL support, not the most intensive tier.

questions.key: Compare an ELL's growth with true peers (same language, proficiency, schooling); a gap in level with normal growth doesn't suggest disability.

questions.stem: In a multi-tiered system of supports (MTSS/RTI), which of the following must a school establish before it concludes that an ELL's lack of progress may reflect a learning disability?
options: That the student has attended U.S. schools for at least five years, the time typically needed to develop academic English
That the student received high-quality, linguistically responsive core instruction, including required ENL services
That the student's parents have confirmed the difficulty is not caused by the family's use of the home language
That the student has reached at least the Expanding level on the NYSESLAT, so that tests given in English will be valid
questions.why: RTI/MTSS rests on ruling out lack of instruction. For an ELL, that means showing that core (Tier 1) instruction was high quality and culturally and linguistically responsive, included the required ENL or bilingual services, and that the student's progress was compared with that of true peers. Only then does insufficient response point toward a possible disability. No minimum number of years or proficiency level is required.

traps.note: No law or regulation requires a set number of years. The CALP timeline describes typical development; it isn't a waiting period.
Home-language use doesn't cause learning difficulties; it supports development. Treating it as a possible cause is a deficit view.
Waiting for English proficiency delays help for students who may have a disability. Valid evaluation comes from assessing in the home language, not from waiting.

questions.key: Before suspecting a disability, verify that the ELL received quality, linguistically responsive Tier 1 instruction and the required ENL services.

questions.stimulus: Note from a parent, translated from Haitian Creole: 'My son Jean is in grade 3. In Haiti his teacher said he could not learn his letters like the other children. Here he still cannot read in Kreyòl or English. Please test him to see if he needs special help.'
questions.stem: The school's RTI team has just begun Tier 2 intervention for Jean. The assistant principal says that all RTI tiers must be completed before any evaluation, especially for an ELL. Which response by the ENL teacher is most appropriate?
options: Agree, since the team cannot rule out limited English proficiency until Jean has completed every RTI tier
Suggest that the parent withdraw the request until Jean reaches the Transitioning level, when testing will be more reliable
Ask the classroom teacher to give an informal English reading test to decide whether the parent's request is justified
Explain that RTI cannot delay or deny an evaluation, so the referral should proceed with consent sought in Haitian Creole
questions.why: Federal guidance under IDEA is clear that RTI/MTSS cannot be used to delay or deny an evaluation, and parents may request an initial evaluation at any time. ELL status is not a reason to wait. Here the parent also reports difficulty learning letters in Haiti and reading Kreyòl, a cross-language red flag. The referral should go forward with communication and consent in the family's language, and interventions can continue at the same time.

traps.note: RTI cannot be used to delay or deny an evaluation. A bilingual evaluation is itself how the team rules out limited English proficiency, and interventions can continue meanwhile; waiting ignores cross-language warning signs.
Discouraging a parent from using the right to request an evaluation is inequitable, and no proficiency level is required before an evaluation.
An informal English reading test measures English, not whether a disability exists, and it can't override a parent's referral.

questions.key: RTI/MTSS can never delay or deny an evaluation; parents may request one at any time, and ELL status is not a reason to wait.

questions.stem: A grade 6 ELL whose home language is Urdu has been referred to the Committee on Special Education (CSE). No Urdu-speaking school psychologist is on staff. Which evaluation plan best meets legal and professional standards?
options: Use a bilingual evaluator, or a trained Urdu interpreter working with the psychologist, plus multiple measures and a language history
Have the psychologist give a standardized English intelligence test while a bilingual aide translates each item into Urdu aloud
Rely on a nonverbal intelligence test alone, since a nonverbal format removes the effects of language and culture from the results
Evaluate the student only in English, since English is the language in which she will receive any special education services
questions.why: IDEA requires evaluations to be provided and administered in the child's native language, in the form most likely to yield accurate information, and it forbids using any single measure as the sole basis for eligibility. When no bilingual evaluator is on staff, the district can contract one or use a trained interpreter working with the psychologist. Translating a standardized test on the spot invalidates its norms, and even nonverbal tests carry cultural and language demands.

traps.note: Translating a standardized test on the spot changes the items and invalidates the norms, and an untrained aide may alter meaning. The scores can't be interpreted.
A nonverbal measure can be one useful piece, but it is not free of culture or language, and IDEA forbids relying on a single measure.
IDEA requires evaluations in the child's native language, in the form most likely to yield accurate information, whatever the language of later services.

questions.key: Evaluate ELLs in the home language (bilingual evaluator or trained interpreter) with multiple measures; never translate standardized tests on the fly.

questions.stem: A grade 3 student with an IEP for autism enrolls in a NYS district from the Dominican Republic, and her Home Language Questionnaire indicates that Spanish is spoken at home. The district convenes a Language Proficiency Team (LPT). Which question is central to the LPT's work?
options: Whether her disability is severe enough to require a more restrictive special education setting than her IEP now provides
Which program her parents prefer (TBE, Dual Language, or ENL), so that her IEP services can be scheduled around it
Whether she may have English acquisition needs, or her disability is the determinant factor in her English proficiency
Whether her special education services already address her English, so that ENL services can be waived for her
questions.why: When a newly enrolled student with an IEP has an HLQ showing a language other than English, NYS sends the case to a Language Proficiency Team, which brings together ESOL/bilingual and special education expertise and the parent. Using evidence such as her language history, records, and evaluations (including any in Spanish), the LPT judges whether she may have English language acquisition needs or whether her disability is the determinant factor. If it finds possible language needs, she takes the NYSITELL; a recommendation not to test goes to the superintendent for a decision.

traps.note: Placement and services for her disability are decisions for the Committee on Special Education. The LPT's question is whether she may have English language acquisition needs.
Program choice comes after a student is identified as an ELL, at the parent orientation. The LPT's question comes first: whether she should take the NYSITELL at all.
ELLs with disabilities are entitled to both ENL and IEP services; special education never lets a district waive required ENL services.

questions.key: The LPT asks whether a student with an IEP may have English language acquisition needs, or whether the disability is the determinant factor.

questions.stem: At the annual review for a grade 5 ELL at the Transitioning level who has a learning disability, a team member proposes ending her ENL services because her schedule already includes resource room and 'special education covers her needs.' Which response is most appropriate?
options: Agree, since under NYS rules a student may receive special education or ENL services, but not both at the same time
Agree, but add ELL testing accommodations to her IEP so that her language needs are still addressed on state tests
Replace her ENL minutes with more resource room time, since her disability is the main source of her language difficulties
Explain that she is entitled to both ENL and special education services and that her IEP must address her language needs
questions.why: ELLs with disabilities are entitled to both the special education services in their IEPs and the ENL or bilingual services required under Part 154; the 2015 federal Dear Colleague Letter likewise rejects 'either-or' policies. IDEA also requires the IEP team to consider the language needs of a child with limited English proficiency. Her ENL and special education teachers should collaborate so that the IEP goals, services, and accommodations address both language development and the disability.

traps.note: There is no 'either-or' rule. ELLs with disabilities must receive both the ENL services required by Part 154 and the services in their IEPs.
Testing accommodations help on tests but don't replace ENL instruction; she remains entitled to her ENL units of study.
This attributes her second-language development to her disability. Language acquisition needs call for ENL instruction, whatever her disability.

questions.key: ELLs with disabilities receive both ENL and special education services, and IDEA requires IEP teams to consider the student's language needs.

questions.stimulus:
Draft IEP annual goal for Amira, grade 7 (home language: Arabic; NYSESLAT level: Emerging; classification: speech or language impairment):
'Amira will independently read and summarize grade-level English texts with 90% accuracy by June.'
questions.stem: The ENL teacher is asked to help revise the goal so that it reflects both Amira's disability and her English proficiency level. Which revision is most appropriate?
options: Amira will use only English during her speech-language sessions, so that she gets maximum exposure to the language of instruction.
Amira will retell key events from grade-level texts using visuals, sentence frames, and home-language support in 4 of 5 trials.
Amira will complete grade 2 phonics and vocabulary worksheets with 90% accuracy, matching her level on an English reading inventory.
Amira will reach the Commanding level on the NYSESLAT by June, so that her IEP no longer needs to address her language needs.
questions.why: IDEA requires IEP teams to consider an ELL's language needs, so goals should be measurable, tied to grade-level standards, and realistic for the student's English proficiency level. The New Language Arts Progressions show what an Emerging student can do with substantial scaffolding, such as retelling with visuals, organizers, sentence frames, and home-language support. The original goal treats Amira as a proficient English reader; the worksheet goal lowers the content, and an English-only rule treats her home language as a problem.

traps.note: Banning the home language treats it as an obstacle. For a student with a language impairment, home-language support often strengthens understanding and transfer.
This trades grade-level content for below-grade worksheets. IEP goals for ELLs should keep access to grade-level standards, with scaffolds.
Jumping from Emerging to Commanding in one year is unrealistic, and a NYSESLAT score is not an instructional goal. Her language needs belong in the IEP while she is an ELL.

questions.key: IEP goals for ELLs should be measurable, tied to grade-level standards, and scaffolded to the proficiency level, with home-language support as needed.

questions.stem: A kindergarten ELL whose home language is Mandarin has said almost nothing in English during his first six weeks of school, though he follows routines and points to answers. His parents say he talks constantly at home in Mandarin with his siblings. His teacher asks whether to refer him for a speech-language evaluation. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Explain that a silent period is typical, and continue visual, low-pressure instruction while monitoring his progress
Refer him now, since six weeks without speaking English is an early warning sign of a speech or language disorder
Require him to answer in English before he can join center activities, so that he becomes motivated to start speaking
Ask his parents to speak only English at home, so that he hears more of the language he will need in school
questions.why: Many beginners go through a silent (preproduction) period in which they build comprehension before speaking; following routines and pointing to answers show that he understands. His rich Mandarin at home is the decisive clue, because a language disorder would show up in the home language too. The teacher should keep providing comprehensible input and low-risk ways to participate, and monitor his progress.

traps.note: His fluent Mandarin at home shows his language system is developing normally. A silent period of several weeks or months is expected for a beginner.
Forcing output during the preproduction stage raises his affective filter and withholds the interaction that will help him begin speaking.
Dropping Mandarin would weaken his strongest language and his family communication; home-language development supports English learning.

questions.key: A silent period is normal for beginners, and fluent home-language speech points away from a language disorder.

questions.stimulus:
District special education identification rates (percentage of students in each group)
Grades | ELLs | Non-ELLs
K–1 | 4% | 9%
2–3 | 10% | 11%
6–8 | 19% | 12%
questions.stem: Which interpretation of these data should the district's ENL and special education leaders investigate first?
options: ELLs develop disabilities at higher rates as they get older, so the pattern reflects accurate identification across grades
The low K–1 rate shows that the district is successfully avoiding the over-identification of its youngest ELLs
Early difficulties may be dismissed as 'just language,' while later academic-language struggles are mistaken for disability
The pattern reflects cultural differences, since families of ELLs are often less willing to accept a disability label
questions.why: Both under- and over-identification harm ELLs. A low early rate can mean that real disabilities are missed because difficulties are attributed to language (a harmful delay). A high rate in later grades can mean that students whose academic language is still developing are mislabeled as disabled. Leaders should examine referral practices, true-peer data, and home-language evaluation rather than accept either rate as accurate.

traps.note: This takes the numbers at face value. Being an ELL doesn't cause disabilities; a sharp shift in rates across grades points to referral practices, not true prevalence.
A rate less than half that of non-ELLs suggests that young ELLs with real disabilities may be missed. Under-identification is a harmful delay, not a success.
This blames families and overgeneralizes about many different cultures, while the grade-by-grade pattern points to decisions made by the school.

questions.key: ELLs face both under-identification (early: 'just language') and over-identification (later: language mistaken for disability); both are harmful.

questions.stem: Under IDEA, which of the following, if it is the determinant factor in a student's difficulties, prevents the team from finding the student eligible for special education?
options: Fewer than five years of schooling in the United States, the time academic English typically requires
A NYSESLAT level below Expanding, which shows that the student is still developing English proficiency
Difficulties that appear in both the home language and English, across school and home settings
A lack of appropriate instruction in reading or math, or the student's limited English proficiency
questions.why: IDEA's exclusionary rule says a child must not be found eligible if the determinant factor is lack of appropriate instruction in reading (including its essential components) or math, or limited English proficiency. That is why teams must document adequate instruction and evaluate in the home language. The rule sets no waiting period; it requires the team to show that language or missing instruction doesn't explain the difficulty.

traps.note: IDEA sets no minimum number of years in U.S. schools. The rule concerns what causes the difficulty, not how long the student has been here.
No NYS or federal rule bars identifying an ELL below a certain NYSESLAT level. An ELL at any level can have a disability.
Difficulties across both languages and settings are a sign that a disability may be present; this option reverses the evidence.

questions.key: IDEA: no eligibility if the determinant factor is lack of appropriate reading or math instruction, or limited English proficiency.

questions.stem: A grade 1 teacher brings concerns to the pre-referral team about Antoni, a Polish-speaking ELL at the Emerging level who is struggling to learn letter sounds and remember sight words. Which information should the team gather first?
options: His developmental, language, and school history from his parents via a Polish interpreter, plus ENL and hearing/vision data
His score on an English-language intelligence test, to see whether his learning ability is in line with his reading achievement
A count of the grade 1 sight words he can read, compared with the benchmark used for every student in grade 1
Classroom behavior notes from his teachers, since school data are more objective than reports from his family
questions.why: Pre-referral for an ELL starts with the information that can separate a language difference from a disability: the child's development and language use at home, prior schooling, and home-language skills; his progress in English compared with true peers, with input from the ENL teacher; and basic hearing and vision screening. Parents are essential informants and should be interviewed through a qualified interpreter.

traps.note: An English IQ test for an Emerging ELL mostly measures English; it can't validly estimate his ability, and it isn't a pre-referral step.
English sight-word data are useful but narrow. Without home-language and developmental information, the team can't tell a difference from a disability.
Parents are essential informants about development and home-language use, the very evidence that separates a language difference from a disability.

questions.key: Pre-referral for ELLs starts with family history (via interpreter), home-language skills, schooling, ENL data, and hearing and vision screening.

questions.stimulus: Student profile, grade 9: Marisol was born in the Bronx and has received ELL services since kindergarten, moving among a bilingual program, Stand-alone ENL, and a year in general education classes with little ENL support. NYSESLAT: Expanding in grades 3–5, Transitioning in grade 6, Expanding in grades 7–8. She remains an ELL. Teachers describe her as articulate and social in English and Spanish. She does not read or write Spanish. Her ELA essays are brief, rely on everyday vocabulary, and contain few transitions or complex sentences.
questions.stem: Which description best characterizes Marisol's profile?
options: A student with a probable language-based learning disability, since she has not exited ELL status after nine years
A SIFE, since years of inconsistent program placement have left her below grade level in academic literacy
A student who should exit ELL status now, since her fluent conversational English shows she has reached proficiency
A Long-Term ELL whose social language is well developed but whose academic language and literacy need explicit teaching
questions.why: NYS defines Long-Term ELLs as students who have completed six or more years of ELL services. Marisol fits the typical LTELL profile: fluent social language (BICS) in two languages but limited academic language and literacy (CALP), after inconsistent programming and no home-language literacy development. The right response is explicit academic language and literacy instruction, not a disability referral or a premature exit.

traps.note: Stalled progress at Expanding with strong oral skills in two languages is the classic LTELL pattern, usually caused by programming, not disability. Nothing here shows difficulties across languages.
SIFE status applies to ELLs with under 12 months in U.S. schools whose prior schooling was interrupted. Marisol has been in U.S. schools since kindergarten.
Exit requires Commanding on the NYSESLAT, or Expanding plus Level 3 on the Grades 3–8 ELA test or 65 on the Regents ELA exam. Conversational fluency is not an exit criterion.

questions.key: LTELL: 6+ years of ELL services, often orally fluent with weak academic literacy; respond with explicit academic language instruction.

questions.stem: A high school is scheduling a group of grade 10 Long-Term ELLs at the Expanding level who are orally fluent in English but failing several content courses. Which program decision is most appropriate?
options: Place them in the newcomer ENL class, where the slower pace and basic vocabulary will rebuild their English foundations
Keep them in grade-level content courses with Integrated ENL, and add a course in academic reading, writing, and discussion
Move them to remedial content classes with simplified texts until their grades improve enough for them to return to regular courses
Replace their ENL services with an extra study hall, since tutoring on homework will help them pass their courses faster
questions.why: LTELLs need rigorous, grade-level content with scaffolds plus targeted instruction in the academic language and literacy they have not yet mastered. Newcomer classes don't match their strong oral English and can feel demeaning; remedial tracks lower expectations and widen gaps; and Expanding students are still entitled to Integrated ENL under Part 154. An academic literacy course designed for LTELLs addresses the real need.

traps.note: Newcomer instruction targets beginners. LTELLs already have strong everyday English; what they lack is academic language, and placing them with newcomers can feel demeaning.
Simplified, remedial courses lower expectations and widen the gap. LTELLs need grade-level content with scaffolds.
Expanding students are still ELLs entitled to Integrated ENL under Part 154; a study hall can't replace required services.

questions.key: LTELLs need grade-level content with Integrated ENL plus targeted academic literacy, not newcomer classes, remedial tracks, or dropped services.

questions.stem: Several grade 8 Long-Term ELLs ask their ENL teacher, 'Why am I still in ENL? I speak English fine.' They have begun to disengage in class. Which response best addresses both their frustration and their language needs?
options: Review each student's NYSESLAT results and writing samples with them, set academic goals together, and track progress
Reassure them that their English is excellent, and shift more class time toward the conversation activities they enjoy most
Explain that state rules require them to attend ENL until they meet the exit criteria and that full participation is expected
Let them work on homework from their content classes during ENL, since the language lessons seem too easy for them
questions.why: LTELLs often don't realize that their remaining needs are academic, not conversational, and that gap fuels frustration. Making the need visible with their own data (NYSESLAT results and writing samples), setting concrete academic-language goals together, and tracking progress builds metacognition and ownership. It treats them as capable partners while keeping the focus on the academic reading and writing that will lead to exit.

traps.note: Conversation is their strength, not their need. More social talk won't build the academic reading and writing that keep them from exiting.
This is accurate, but it doesn't address their frustration or help them see what they still need to learn.
Turning ENL into homework time abandons the targeted academic language instruction LTELLs need.

questions.key: Engage LTELLs by making their academic-language needs visible with their own data and setting goals together.

questions.stimulus:
Excerpt from a grade 10 Long-Term ELL's argument essay on lowering the voting age to 16:
'So basically teens should vote because like they know stuff too. Like my cousin she's 16 and she knows way more about politics then a lot of grown ups. And also it's not fair cuz we gotta follow the laws but we can't even pick who makes them.'
questions.stem: Which instructional focus would best address the most significant need shown in this excerpt?
options: Daily grammar worksheets on commas and sentence fragments, assigned until the student's error rate drops below a set level
Marking every informal word and grammatical error in red, so that the student can see exactly what to avoid next time
Mentor-text analysis and joint construction showing how to move from conversational to academic register in arguments
Independent reading of high-interest novels, since wide reading will gradually improve the student's writing over the year
questions.why: The student has a real argument (a claim, an example, and a reason grounded in fairness) but writes in a conversational register: 'like,' 'stuff,' 'cuz,' 'gotta,' and strings of 'and also.' This is typical of LTELLs, whose everyday English is strong while academic register is underdeveloped. Analyzing mentor texts and jointly constructing paragraphs (a genre-based approach) makes the features of academic register visible and gives students guided practice: precise vocabulary, transitions, and evidence.

traps.note: Mechanics drills apart from real writing won't teach register, which is the main gap. The student's ideas are strong; the language of academic argument is missing.
Marking everything overwhelms the student and focuses on surface errors instead of teaching the academic language that would replace them.
Wide reading helps, but on its own it rarely makes academic register visible. LTELLs need explicit instruction in how academic arguments are worded.

questions.key: LTELL writing often has strong ideas in a conversational register; teach academic register explicitly with mentor texts and joint construction.

questions.stem: Research on Long-Term ELLs most often identifies which of the following as a major contributor to their long-term status?
options: Continued use of the home language with family members, which limits the students' exposure to English
Inconsistent programs across the years and little explicit instruction in academic language and literacy
An undiagnosed learning disability, which explains why most Long-Term ELLs have not reached proficiency
Low motivation to learn English, since most Long-Term ELLs are satisfied with their social language skills
questions.why: Studies of LTELLs, such as Laurie Olsen's work, point to schooling factors: moving among bilingual, ENL, and general education settings without a coherent plan; instruction that never explicitly taught academic language and literacy; and, often, no home-language literacy development. LTELL status is largely a product of programming, not of the home language, motivation, or disability.

traps.note: Home-language use is not the cause. Many LTELLs actually lack home-language literacy, which would have supported their English.
Most LTELLs do not have disabilities; their stalled progress usually reflects programming. Assuming a disability leads to over-referral.
This blames the students and overgeneralizes. When disengagement occurs, it often follows years of ineffective programming.

questions.key: LTELL status is largely a product of schooling: inconsistent programs and no explicit academic language and literacy instruction.

questions.stem: A grade 11 Long-Term ELL who speaks Spanish fluently at home but has never studied it formally is enrolled in a Spanish for Heritage Speakers course. Her counselor proposes replacing it with a second period of remedial English reading. Which response best reflects research and NYS priorities?
options: Keep the heritage course, since Spanish literacy skills transfer to English and can lead toward the Seal of Biliteracy
Approve the change, since every period spent on Spanish takes time away from the English she needs to meet the exit criteria
Approve the change, but encourage her to keep speaking Spanish at home, since oral use is enough to maintain her home language
Move her into Spanish 1 instead, since a beginner course will teach the formal grammar that heritage speakers have not learned
questions.why: Literacy skills and academic concepts developed in the home language transfer to English (Cummins' interdependence), so building Spanish literacy supports her English academic growth rather than competing with it. A heritage course also builds on an existing asset, affirms identity, and can put her on the path to the NYS Seal of Biliteracy. Beginner Spanish ignores her oral proficiency, and cutting the course reflects the 'time on English' fallacy.

traps.note: This is the 'time on English' fallacy. Home-language literacy supports English academic literacy rather than competing with it.
Speaking Spanish at home is valuable, but it won't develop the literacy and academic language that transfer to English and that she currently lacks.
A beginner course ignores her oral proficiency. Heritage speakers need instruction that builds literacy and academic register on the language they already have.

questions.key: Home-language literacy courses help LTELLs and heritage speakers: the skills transfer to English and build toward the Seal of Biliteracy.

questions.stem: A district notices that ELLs are rarely identified for its gifted and talented program, which uses a single English-language verbal reasoning test with a fixed cutoff score. Which change would most improve equitable identification of ELLs?
options: Allow ELLs to take the English verbal test once they reach the Commanding level on the NYSESLAT
Provide bilingual glossaries during the existing verbal test while keeping the same cutoff score for everyone
Use multiple criteria, such as nonverbal and home-language measures, local norms, and informed nominations
Create a separate, slower-paced enrichment class for ELLs so that they are not compared with native speakers
questions.why: A single English verbal test with a fixed cutoff mostly measures English proficiency, so it systematically screens out gifted ELLs. Equitable identification uses multiple measures: nonverbal and home-language assessments, local or 'true peer' norms, portfolios, and teacher and parent nominations guided by checklists of how giftedness appears in ELLs. It never requires English proficiency first.

traps.note: Waiting for English proficiency excludes gifted ELLs during the years when they would benefit, and it is a main cause of underrepresentation.
A glossary helps a little, but a single English verbal test still mostly measures English proficiency, so the barrier remains.
A slower-paced class lowers expectations and segregates ELLs instead of identifying and serving their advanced abilities.

questions.key: Identify gifted ELLs with multiple criteria (nonverbal, home-language, local norms, informed nominations), never requiring English proficiency first.

questions.stimulus:
Grade 3 teacher's notes on Yousef (home language: Arabic; NYSESLAT: Transitioning; second year in U.S. schools)
- Moved from Entering to Transitioning in one year, faster than classmates with similar backgrounds.
- Invents his own strategies for multistep math problems and explains them in Arabic to a classmate.
- Writes long, imaginative stories in Arabic with complex plots.
- Answers questions in short English phrases with frequent grammatical errors.
questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the notes?
options: His English grammar errors and short answers suggest that a gifted referral would be premature until he reaches Expanding
His strengths appear mainly in Arabic, so they show bilingual ability rather than the advanced reasoning gifted programs serve
His math strategies show giftedness in mathematics only, so he should get math enrichment rather than a full gifted screening
His rapid English growth, inventive problem solving, and complex Arabic writing are signs of giftedness that warrant nomination
questions.why: Giftedness in ELLs often shows up in the rate of English acquisition compared with true peers, in creative problem solving, and in sophisticated use of the home language, not in polished English. Yousef's English errors are typical for his level and say nothing about his ability. Requiring English proficiency before nomination is a major cause of ELL underrepresentation in gifted programs.

traps.note: His English errors are typical for his level and say nothing about his ability. Waiting for English proficiency is a major reason gifted ELLs go unidentified.
Complex reasoning and writing in Arabic are evidence of advanced ability. Discounting home-language performance treats his first language as if it didn't count.
Math enrichment may help, but the evidence also includes unusually rapid language learning and sophisticated writing, so a full screening is warranted.

questions.key: Gifted ELL indicators: fast English growth compared with true peers, creative problem solving, rich home-language use; nominate without waiting for English.

questions.stem: A grade 6 ELL at the Transitioning level in an advanced math class solves problems accurately but writes very brief explanations of her reasoning. Her math teacher suggests moving her to a standard math class until her English improves. Which response by the ENL teacher is most appropriate?
options: Agree, since written explanation is a required part of the advanced course and she cannot yet meet that standard
Recommend keeping her in the class and co-planning supports such as sentence frames, word banks, and oral rehearsal
Suggest that she be excused from written explanations and graded only on the accuracy of her answers to problems
Recommend a special education referral, since the gap between her math skills and her writing may signal a disability
questions.why: Her accurate problem solving shows that she belongs in advanced math; the brief explanations reflect developing academic English, which is exactly what scaffolds address. Keeping her in the class and co-planning language supports, such as frames for mathematical explanations, math word banks, and talking before writing, maintains rigor while building the language of mathematical reasoning. Removing her until she is proficient is an equity problem.

traps.note: Removing her until she is proficient denies her an advanced placement she has earned. The gap is language, which can be scaffolded.
Dropping the explanations lowers expectations and skips the academic language of mathematical reasoning she needs to develop.
A gap between strong math and brief English writing is typical for a Transitioning ELL; it doesn't suggest a disability.

questions.key: Keep capable ELLs in advanced classes and scaffold the language; don't remove them until they are proficient.

questions.stimulus: Grade 10 student profile: Kasia was born in Brooklyn to Polish-speaking parents. She speaks Polish with her grandparents and follows family conversations easily, but she rarely reads or writes in Polish. English is her dominant language. When she enrolled in kindergarten, her Home Language Questionnaire indicated Polish, and she scored Commanding on the NYSITELL.
questions.stem: Which description of Kasia is most accurate?
options: She is a heritage speaker of Polish who is not an ELL, and her Polish is an asset the school can help her develop
She is an ELL, since a language other than English is spoken at home and her HLQ indicated Polish at enrollment
She is a Long-Term ELL, since she has been using two languages throughout her ten years of schooling in NYS
Her Polish is incomplete compared with that of speakers raised in Poland, so it should not be counted as a skill
questions.why: A heritage speaker grew up with a home language, often with strong listening and speaking but limited literacy, and is frequently English-dominant. Heritage speakers may or may not be ELLs. In NYS, ELL status comes from NYSITELL (and later NYSESLAT) results, not from the HLQ alone, and Kasia scored Commanding at entry. Her Polish is a valuable asset that a heritage-language course could develop toward biliteracy and the Seal of Biliteracy.

traps.note: The HLQ only determines who takes the NYSITELL. Kasia scored Commanding, so she was never identified as an ELL.
A Long-Term ELL has completed six or more years of ELL services. Kasia never received services; being bilingual is not ELL status.
Heritage speakers' language is real, valuable competence, often with strong listening and speaking. Calling it 'incomplete' devalues an asset schools should build on.

questions.key: Heritage speakers grew up with a home language, are often English-dominant, may not be ELLs, and bring an asset worth developing.

questions.stimulus:
Grade 5 writing sample. The student is a native speaker of English whose home variety is African American English (AAE):
'Every Saturday my grandma be making pancakes. My brother always hungry so he eat like five. Then we go to the park.'
questions.stem: A colleague says the student 'doesn't know basic grammar' and suggests a speech-language referral. Which response best reflects current understanding of language variation?
options: Agree to the referral, since a native English speaker should not be making subject-verb agreement errors by grade 5
Recommend NYSITELL screening, since consistent use of nonstandard English suggests the student may be an ELL
Explain that the sentences follow consistent AAE rules, and use contrastive analysis to teach Standard English for writing
Correct each nonstandard form whenever it appears in speech or writing, so the student learns that home patterns are wrong
questions.why: African American English is a rule-governed variety of English. Habitual 'be' (marking a repeated action), absence of the copula ('my brother always hungry'), and absence of third-person -s ('he eat') follow systematic patterns, so they are dialect differences, not disorders; ASHA's position is that no dialect of English is a disorder. Contrastive analysis, which compares home and school patterns side by side (as in Wheeler and Swords' code-switching approach), adds Standard English for academic settings without devaluing the student's home variety.

traps.note: Dialect features are not disorders. ASHA's position is that no dialect of English is a speech or language disorder.
Speaking a variety of English doesn't make a student an ELL. The NYSITELL is given when the HLQ indicates a language other than English.
Labeling home patterns 'wrong' devalues the student's language and identity and tends to backfire. The goal is to add Standard English, not to replace AAE.

questions.key: AAE and other dialects are rule-governed: use contrastive analysis to add Standard English for academic contexts, and never refer or stigmatize.

questions.stem: At registration, a parent from Guatemala tells staff through a Spanish interpreter that the family speaks 'un dialecto' at home and Spanish only 'a little.' Further conversation shows that the home language is K'iche'. Which understanding should guide the school's next steps?
options: Since the parent understands some Spanish, Spanish interpretation is sufficient for the HLQ interview and for future meetings
K'iche' is a regional dialect of Spanish, so the student's Spanish-speaking classmates can serve as language buddies
Because K'iche' is mainly an oral language, the school should focus on English and limit the use of the home language
K'iche' is a distinct Mayan language, not a Spanish dialect, so the school should record it and seek K'iche' interpretation
questions.why: Many Indigenous languages of Latin America, such as K'iche', Q'anjob'al, and Mixteco, are distinct languages, not dialects of Spanish, even though speakers sometimes call them 'dialecto,' a label that reflects a history of low social status. A K'iche'-speaking student may be learning both Spanish and English as additional languages. Accurately identifying the home language shapes the HLQ interview, interpretation for the family, assessment, and instruction.

traps.note: A parent who knows 'a little' Spanish may not fully understand an interview or meeting. Meaningful communication calls for the family's strongest language whenever possible.
K'iche' is a separate Mayan language, unrelated to Spanish. Calling it a dialect reflects its social status, not linguistic fact.
K'iche' has a written alphabet, and every language, oral or written, is a resource for learning. Limiting it treats the home language as a problem.

questions.key: Indigenous languages such as K'iche', Q'anjob'al, and Mixteco are distinct languages, not Spanish dialects; identify them accurately and don't assume Spanish.

questions.stimulus: In grade 4, Mei scored Expanding on the NYSESLAT and Level 3 on the Grades 3–8 ELA test.
questions.stem: Mei has met the NYS exit criteria. Which describes what NYS requires for her in grades 5 and 6?
options: Full ELL services until she scores Commanding, since a score of Expanding is not by itself an exiting level
Continued support, such as 90 minutes a week of Integrated ENL, plus ELL testing accommodations for two years
Continued ENL services for four years, since federal law keeps former ELs in the EL subgroup for four years
Testing accommodations for two years, but no further instructional support now that she is a former ELL
questions.why: Mei exited through the second NYS path: Expanding on the NYSESLAT plus Level 3 on the Grades 3–8 ELA test. As a former ELL, she receives two years of continued support (in grades K–8, 90 minutes a week of Integrated ENL or other approved former-ELL services) and keeps ELL testing accommodations for two years. The 4-year figure is a federal accountability rule, not a service requirement.

traps.note: Expanding plus Level 3 on the Grades 3–8 ELA test (or 65 on the Regents ELA) is an exit path; Commanding is not the only route.
ESSA lets states keep former ELs in the EL subgroup for up to 4 years for accountability reporting. NYS services and accommodations last 2 years.
Accommodations are only half of it. Former ELLs also receive continued instructional support, such as Integrated ENL, for two years.

questions.key: Former ELLs get 2 years of continued support (90 min/week in K–8) and testing accommodations; ESSA's 4 years is for accountability only.

questions.stem: A grade 8 science teacher reports that a former ELL who exited last year is struggling to understand the textbook and write lab conclusions. He says, 'She's not an ELL anymore, so she should be able to keep up,' and asks whether she should be referred for special education. Which response by the ENL teacher is most appropriate?
options: Agree to a referral, since difficulties that continue after exit can no longer be explained by second-language acquisition
Explain that former ELLs no longer qualify for language support, so she should attend general tutoring like other students
Explain that academic language keeps developing after exit, and co-plan science-language scaffolds as former-ELL support
